time_of_day: Early evening — first prahar of night (6pm to 9pm)
aaroh: Sa Re Ga Ma# Pa Dha Ni Sa
avaroh: Sa Ni Dha Pa Ma# Ga Re Sa
notes_used: All shuddh plus Ma teevra (sharp fourth) — the teevra Ma is what defines this raag
characteristic_pakad: Re Ga Ma# Re Sa, Ni Re Ga, Pa Dha Ni Sa
emotional_resonance: tiredness after a long day at work
need to transition from work-mode to home-mode
wanting to connect with family but feeling too drained
feeling emotionally flat or numb at evening
wanting to feel beautiful or hopeful again
mild depression that arrives with sunset
therapy_note: Yaman is the most universally loved of all Hindustani raags — it is the gateway raag that every student learns first, and yet masters spend decades exploring it. The teevra Ma (sharp fourth) is the raag's defining note — it creates a slight lift, an elevation, like light catching the edge of a cloud at sunset. Yaman feels open, welcoming and luminous. Singing it at dusk reconnects the spirit to beauty after a mundane day.

bollywood_references.title: Jab Deep Jale Aana
bollywood_references.note: Pure Yaman — the teevra Ma is clearly audible throughout

classical_reference: The most-recorded raag in Hindustani music. Pandit Bhimsen Joshi, Ustad Rashid Khan, and virtually every major artist has recorded Yaman. Bandish: 'Eri Aali Piya Bin'
notes_for_vocalist: The teevra Ma (sharp fourth) is what makes this Yaman — use it clearly and without hesitation. In aalaap, approach Ma# from below with gentle oscillation. Ni is the samvadi and creates a beautiful tension with Sa. The raag has great scope — from gentle thumri to deep khayal. Beginners often flatten the Ma accidentally — be deliberate about keeping it sharp.
